en: Preface to the *Shiqian* (Explanatory Notes on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra-śāstra*) Composed by Tian-tai Ling-yao Quan-zhang. The Preface to the *Shiqian* states:
"Like threads threading beads, the words and principles are clearly manifest; there is no need for further annotation. Recently, however, I have observed..."
In publishing commentaries, or in the practice of "shifu" (divination by covering), the distinctions between host and guest, or peripheral and central, have become disordered;

or when several chapters are treated as a single unit, the categories of mother and child, or grandfather and grandson, are somewhat violated. It is like the sun shining in the heavens, only briefly obscured by a passing cloud.
To cleanse even the finest specks of dust and clarify the meaning of the text’s principles—this is the origin of the preface to the *Qiān* (Commentary), which elucidates these points.

Title II. I. Preface to the Title.
Regarding the Preface to the *Yuanqi* (Origins) of the *Shiqian* (Explanatory Commentary): Master Jingxi has already composed a preface for the *Shiqian*, as seen in the following passage:

"Formerly, on Mount Tiantai, I recorded one chapter from among the various questions posed to me below the *Shiqian*. This current preface by my Master not only introduces the *Shiqian*, but furthermore...

This preface provides a detailed explanation of the origins (*nidāna*) of the *Zhiguang fenzan chao* (Commentary on the Subdivisions of the *Mohe zhiguan*). Generally speaking, each literary composition has its own particular emphasis;

in this preface, the two characters "yuanqi" (origins) are paramount. Regarding "origins," as stated in the *Zhi guan*: that which can produce is the "condition" (*yuan*), and that which is produced is the "arising" (*qi*).

The preceding chapters constitute the condition, while the subsequent chapters constitute the arising. As for "condition," it refers to the causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*); as for "arising," it refers to that which is...

Regarding the dharma of arising: among all phenomena—both mundane and supramundane, defiled and pure, including both the primary and secondary—the there is none that does not arise from causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Although causes and conditions act as the initiators and producers, they are nonetheless adventitious and secondary;

whereas the phenomena produced, though appearing later, are the primary and essential reality. This is like the emission of light while entering meditative absorption (*samādhi*), which acts as the condition for [the subsequent] arising.
The method of opening the three to reveal the one arose from the condition of King Ajātaśatru’s parricide;

the method of giving rise to the sixteen sublime contemplations arose from the condition of the cruelty of Jie and Zhou; the method of layering ice and firm adherence arose from the condition of the freezing cold that causes the earth to crack;
and now, by means of the condition of this profound and vast esoteric record, [the following] arises...
The method of initiating the *Shiqian* (Commentary on the Sub-commentary) was established. Zhiyi (the Wise One) brought peace to the ancestral tradition, thereby severing [the cycle of] conditions;
Jingxi initiated the method capable of upholding the lineage of the Way. It did not stop there:

because Master Tan possessed talent that was adaptable to all situations, he initiated the method capable of providing exegesis. Because the times were in turmoil and difficult to propagate widely, he initiated...

Regarding the method of inquiring by means of divination sticks (*zhān*): it was because those who sought the ultimate depths were unable to attain awakening upon merely observing the sticks that [the Master] gave rise to the method of compiling these teachings into ten fascicles.

Not only does the formal narrative detail the beginning and end, but even the two characters "yuanqi" (causal origination) used throughout—whether in concluding explanations or in composing prefaces—are themselves "yuanqi. Why is this? Because at a later time, following the Way...

Through the conditions of his early years spent amidst worldly dust, he gave rise to the capacity to compose the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the *Śāstra*), which strikes forth and activates [the meaning].
Through the conditions of his youthful involvement in secular affairs, he gave rise to the humility of a disciple’s sense of shame.

Thus, within the records of these events, through the condition of the Heavenly King being unable to assemble a multitude to propagate the Sūtra, there arose the method by which the *Shiqian* was successfully completed in the following year. Throughout this interval, there were both incidental and primary [conditions].
The distinction between subject and object is clear and orderly. This is because the title specifically establishes the two characters "yuanqi" (causal origination) as the point of primary emphasis;

this is what is meant by the "mind of the composition. Therefore, although there are over three hundred characters in the main body of the text, from beginning to end they only elucidate "causal origination," with nothing else said. By clarifying it in this manner, the author’s intention is finally made manifest.
△ Second, the Preface Author:
The monk Pumen of Junshan, a disciple of Men-shi Yueyang He Jie.
Jie served as the Magistrate of Yixing and subsequently resided there as a sojourner. Junshan is [located in] Yixing.

Regarding the name "Xingxiang" (Reviving the Village): as a bhikṣu in his causal stage, he sustained his entire body by begging for alms; as one who has attained the fruit, he is worthy of offerings from humans and devas, capable of eliminating the calamity of famine.
As for the name "Pumenzi" (Son of the Universal Gate): some take "Pu" (Universal) as the name, for according to the present preface, only the single character "Pu" appears;
others take "Men" (Gate) as the name, for according to the *Tongji*, he is simply referred to as "Menshi" (Master of the Gate). However, both characters are indeed names.
The preface to "Sending the Śramaṇa Jiānxū Back to Yuè," in Volume 726 of the *Wényuàn yīnghuá*, by Liáng Sù, states:
"Among the eminent monks of the southeast, there is Pǔmén Yuánhào, with whom I am a very close friend.
When we meet, he kindly speaks of my vulgar self’s restless and mundane condition; let us instead cleanse the defilements of our minds and pledge ourselves to one another."
This refers to the "State of Nothingness. Regarding the term *shuci* (屬辭): it is based on the Master’s composition of the *Chunqiu*.
*Shu* means to string together or compile. There is a view that because he was commissioned by his teacher to compose it, it was named *Shuci*; this is incorrect.

△ Second, the introductory text has two parts: first, the preface; second, the record of events. The first part has two sections. First, a detailed explanation of the causes and conditions for the sub-commentary (*shiqian*), which further has two parts.
First, the presentation of the person and the teaching explained as the conditions, which further has two parts. First, the transmission of the Dharma and the severing of conditions.

The four teachings are arranged in sequence; the principles of their expansion and condensation are contained therein. Since the ten disciples have passed away, the merit of their profound assistance for humanity has been severed.

Desiring to introduce the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary), one must first present the fundamental text that the *Shiqian* explains: namely, the *Fahua Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra). "Xuan" (Profound)...
In the exposition of the meaning, whenever a single dharma is enumerated, it must first be explained by means of the four teachings of the transformative method (*huàfǎ sìjiào*).

Only then does one employ the five periods of the transformative ritual (*huàyí wǔshí*) to clearly distinguish and clarify the process of revelation (*kāi*). Taking the four teachings as an example, they inherently encompass the general principles for distinguishing and revealing the five periods of the transformative ritual;

therefore, it is said that "the four teachings are arranged such that the principle of opening and closing is contained within them. "Opening" (*kāi*) refers precisely to the bestowal of provisional means (*shìquán*).

This refers to how, from a single path of purity, there emerge two, three, and four [teachings]. Once the capacities of those to be converted have matured, they are all delivered and liberated by means of the One Great Vehicle (Ekayāna).
In summary, the former four flavors—the coarse—are opened up, merged, and set aside, as they all return to the wondrousness of the One Vehicle.
While the Two Truths, Three Paths, and Four Fruits were not unified in the past, they are now all unified. This is because...

When it is said that "the wise person's profound meaning is accomplished," it means that the Tathāgata’s overarching intent for his entire career—encompassing the dispensations, expositions, and assemblies—is set forth therein.
As the *Xici* (Appended Statements) of the *Book of Changes* says: "When Qian and Kun are arrayed, the *Yi* (Change) is contained within them."

This refers to the Patriarch Zhi’s pioneering of the profound meaning (*xuanyi*). As for the merit of his subtle elucidation, which was on the verge of being lost to others, the Great Master’s *xuanyi* were all expounded from his very seat.
It was thanks to Zhǎng’ān’s talent for comprehensive memorization that they were compiled into written form.
"Elucidation" (*zàn*) here is like the "eulogy" (*zàn*) in the phrase, "When Confucius composed the *Chunqiu*, even You and Xia could not provide a eulogy. Zhǎng’ān compiled...
In compiling or privately annotating [this work], he either cited scriptural passages or provided commentaries;

it was not merely that he was capable of redacting the collection, but in truth, he served as a primary chronicler who provided profound and subtle assistance to the Master’s school. The ancestral master An’s name was Guanding;

he was the son of the Prince of Shizhu. Therefore, the Master’s biographer listed him among the "Ten Sons" to form a pair with the aforementioned four teachings. The subsequent text states: "Mysterious..."

"Extensive and profound records" refers to the Great Master (Zhiyi); "records" refers to Zhāng'ān (Guanding). This single volume of the *Xuánwén* was produced through the collaboration of teacher and disciple, serving as the foundational text for the commentary in the *Shìqiān*.

When it was said that this [text] was on the verge of being lost, it meant that once Zhāng'ān had passed away, it would have been difficult to find anyone capable of transmitting the lineage of the Dharma.
It was Jīngxī who, not long after, was able to transmit the succession of the Way; thus, he is the one who could transmit the Dharma.

The person who unifies [the lineage] was precisely the one who severed the conditions for [such] attachments. The formal explanation is concluded. Furthermore, [the text] has been cleansed of even the finest specks of dust.

It is solely because Master En’s letter regarding the "Ten Sons" (Shizi) is somewhat obscure in its phrasing that the masters of the Shanjia school have offered various interpretations, like those who guess at hidden objects.
Now, I shall clarify this by following the specific indications. Formerly, Master Biaozhao of Wuxia identified the Ten Sons as the sons of a Bodhisattva.
According to the *Fahua xuanyi*, there are ten or twenty [sons]; the ten refer to bodhisattvas, while the twenty point to those of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*).
Master Tangqi identifies the ten sons as the disciples of Zhiyi. According to the initial section of the *Miaofa lianhua jing xuanyi*, Zhiyi was indeed the son endowed with these ten virtues.
Master Jitan identifies them as the ten great disciples. This was transmitted by the three elder brothers Wuzu, Jieben, and Han Yue. Yi.

Master An Yuan refuted his [the opponent's] violation of the text and loss of its intent, as well as his irreverent treatment of the former sages. He pointed out three errors: first, a narrowness of perspective;
second, a deficiency in reasoning; and third, the aforementioned faults. However, Master Yi-an was adept at criticizing others but ignorant of self-examination;

he thus adhered to the ten disciples of the Guanzhong school as the "Ten Sons" and alone proclaimed his own views as an indelible, definitive case for all eternity. Now, it is said that the Great Master spoke of the profound mystery (*xuan*).

The *Yi* (Meanings) was compiled with profound commentary by Zhizhe [Zhanran]. Once these two patriarchs had passed away, Master Zhan left behind the Master Tan, who was able to transmit the lineage of the Dharma;
his *Xuanji* (Profound Record) is already deep. Furthermore, there arose the Master Shi, who could interpret the *Xuanji* through his *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary);

he linked these works together like a string of black pearls without losing their connection. If one were to single out the "Ten Sons" [the disciples of Zhizhe] and promote Zhizhe while relegating Zhizhe’s profound commentary to the region of Guanzhong, then...

To extinguish the legacy of the Patriarch and disrupt the continuity of the lineage—where the principles and expressions are so disordered—is it not a violation of the orderly succession of the profound commentaries (*xuānqiān*)?
To instead drag in others to complete the count of successors, thereby eclipsing the great merit of Master Zhi’an, is egregious.

Furthermore, regarding the commentary on the passage "the lineage of the ten sons was about to end," you claim that this conversely reveals that Zhiyi (Zhìzhě) succeeded him; yet, within the *Xuányì*, the Great Master [Zhiyi] himself...

The various masters of the Southern Dynasties who refuted [this view] all agreed on this single point: "Among the commentaries of past and present, all consider Guangzhai’s interpretation to be the most excellent.
When observing the Southern school’s exegesis of the *Mahāyāna*, it is seen that they largely follow Sengzhao and Kumārajīva;

since Sengzhao and Kumārajīva frequently adhered to the 'comprehensive' (tong) meaning, how could Guangzhai’s profound explanation possibly be far removed from it? Now, I shall first challenge Guangzhai, and the others will fall before my argument like soldiers facing the wind. Thus said Jingxi.
The "Four Sons of Guanzhong" were Sengsheng, Daosheng, Daorong, and Daorui. Later generations have inherited and employed the doctrines of these four masters;
yet, if one evaluates them by contemporary standards, their views mostly lean toward the "Accommodated" (Tong) school.

Based on this, since the Great Master [Sengzhao] had already refuted and dismantled the various theories of the Guanzhong masters, for us now to follow in their footsteps would surely be to disparage our own Patriarch. Furthermore, regarding the preceding four periods...
Regarding the sutras: if a sutra has been opened and revealed by the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it is appropriate to interpret it according to the intent of the *Lotus Sutra*.

To fail to hear this opening and revealing of the perfect sutra, and instead employ "common" (universal) meanings to provide a profound commentary, constitutes an error in interpretation. There are five such faults:

first, it suppresses the founding patriarch [Zhiyi] while conversely inheriting the errors of the Guanzhong school that he had already refuted; second, it destroys the merit of Zhanran’s profound commentary; third, it drags in the Guanzhong school indiscriminately...
There are five types of failure: first, the failure of dwelling upon one's own achievements; second, the failure of confusing the lineage of transmission within a single family;

third, the failure of the master of the Exoteric Gate to lack proficiency in literary composition; fourth, the failure of not knowing how to provide commentaries and explanations that prioritize establishing names according to their meaning so that the logic of the original text flows coherently;

and fifth, the failure of recklessly inserting extraneous material merely to fill a quota, thereby muddling the structural order. How could one possibly allow such things to disrupt the fundamental framework?
△ Second, regarding the two points on the profound nature of the Dharma being still obstructed by conditions: First, the point that the profundity of the Dharma requires interpretation.
Only through the three turnings is the cycle complete; the One Vehicle carries and guides. The scriptural text is manifest yet concise, while the profound commentary is expansive and deep.
Tracing the source to the explanations in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning), this refers to the *Lotus Sūtra*.

The "three turnings" refer to the three turnings demonstrated at the Deer Park—namely, the turning that shows, the turning that encourages, and the turning that realizes—which were for the sake of those with inferior capacities who were transformed through the provisional (*upāya*). Regarding the phrase "finally reaching completion" (*suizhou*):

if one reads the character "suí" (遂) here as a "virtual" (*xū*) word, it feels even more harmonious and integrated. However, if one explains it as a "real" (*shí*) word, it must likewise be interpreted in accordance with the context.

The purport of the sutra is as follows: when the Wheel of Dharma was turned three times, the five bhikṣus, the twelve hundred, and others all realized and entered [the truth] upon hearing these words.

This was thus the Tathāgata’s intention in employing provisional means (upāya); hence the word "suì" (thereby/thus). Furthermore, it is not only the Three Vehicles at the Deer Park that are provisional;

rather, everything bestowed during the preceding four periods of teaching is without exception provisional. This is because the Vaipulya (fangděng) teachings merely censure and reject this Lesser Vehicle.

The vehicle (*yāna*). Prajñā merely refines and purifies this Hīnayāna. Once the faculties of those in the Hīnayāna have matured, the Tathāgata’s intention to employ skillful means (*upāya*) to gather and transform beings through past conditions has been fulfilled; thus it is called "complete" (*zhou*).

In this assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the former employment of skillful means is proclaimed, yet without pointing to what was opened, how could the reality (*bhūtārtha*) be revealed? Thereafter, one immediately uses the One Great Vehicle (*ekamahāyāna*) to deliver them.

To liberate them. This is called the "Vehicle of the Single Vehicle" (Ekayāna), which initially unfolds the various vehicles from the Single Vehicle; now, it reunites those various vehicles so that they return to the Single Vehicle.
Truly, there is nothing that does not flow forth from this Dharma-realm, and there is nothing that does not return to this Dharma-realm.

This refers precisely to the two characters "opening" and "closing" mentioned above. Regarding "carrying and guiding": causing the various sons to each ride upon the great vehicle to enter the secret treasury is "carrying";
furthermore, causing them to travel through the four quarters to increase the Way and diminish birth is "guiding.
Yi-an’s division of the three phrases of turning into the Trace Gate and the phrase of the One Vehicle into the Origin Gate is unfounded and preposterous; this must be understood.

The principle of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) penetrates both the Provisional (迹, *jaku*) and the Real (本, *hon*). Those for whom the Dharma wheel was turned three times are truly the ones to be enlightened.
Why then do you drag in the small, provisional [teachings] as the Gate of the Trace (*jakumon*), while relegating the One Vehicle to the Gate of the Source (*honmon*)?

Consequently, based on the scriptural text, he concludes by stating the reasons for producing this commentary (*shakusho*) to explain it: "In the Lotus Sutra, the scriptural text is explicit, yet its underlying intent is obscure. (From the *Genki*). Regarding the wording...

It is vast and expansive, yet its principles and meanings are profound and subtle. Were it not for Jingxi’s *Shiqian* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning), how could one possibly understand and clarify it?
△ Second, the conditions for explaining [the text] due to the obstruction of the capacity of learners:
those who have recently begun their studies find it difficult to peer into its depths; even those seeking instruction through the *Mengqiu* remain obstructed.

Because the profound and deep records of the Xuan are so vast, even those who seek instruction remain obstructed; it is only through the use of divination and commentary that they may attain understanding.
Regarding the second line of the Meng hexagram: "It is not I who seek the ignorant youth, but the ignorant youth who seeks me. All of the above concerns the person and the method of transmission.

That human beings must depend on Jingxi [Zhanran] for its emergence, and that its profound mysteries must be explained by the *Shu* (Commentary), constitutes the causal conditions for the production of this *Shu*;
these matters are all incidental and peripheral, and not the primary subject of this preface.
△ Second, the two aspects of the persons and teachings capable of transmitting and explaining [the Dharma]: 1. The person capable of transmitting the lineage of the Way.
"Returning before one has gone far" depends upon the timing; our master craftsman, Master Zhànrán, was such a person.

The Great Master Zhanran’s prophetic record states that after the person [Huisi] had passed away, he would not remain distant before returning; subsequently, Jingxi was born, the one capable of transmitting the lineage of the two patriarchs.

Thus, it is said that he was the destined successor. This corresponds to the hexagram *Fu*, where the masses of yin have been stripped away and a single yang returns—its realization depends upon the timing.
This refers to the principle that "every five hundred years, a true king must arise," and within that interval...
There must have been those who were renowned in their time. After the Second Patriarch had passed away, Jingxi happened to be born among them.
"Zhanran" is the name of Jingxi; this follows the rule of not avoiding names when composing formal texts.

△ Second, the section on seeking the Dharma through the commentary on the sub-commentary (*Shiqian*) has two parts: first, the formal explanation of the origins of the commentary; second, the compilation of the origins of the commentary.
As in Jingxi’s original preface, this too is divided into two sections. Previously, while at Mount Tiantai, I recorded notes on the sub-commentary for various inquirers;
I did not have the leisure to investigate the flow of the text in order to compose a formal preface to the commentary. Later, upon my return...

The *Vidhāna-cheda*, the *Tianfu-shi* (Skin Adornment), and so forth, were compiled into written works. Now, within the preface of the Master [Zhiyi], there are also two chapters. The first two [chapters] consist of:

first, a detailed explanation of the conditions for the commentary (*zhuan-yuan*); and second, which is further divided into two: first, the conditions for possessing the requisite talent as the capable commentator (*neng-shi-yuan*).

Master Gong was exceptionally gifted from childhood; when he reached the age of "studying with purpose," his fame was established. His profound understanding arose from within his own mind, and his vast learning surpassed that of his predecessors.
There was nothing he could not master, for he received all things with an empty mind. From Mount Bitan to Guoqing Temple, those who followed him were as numerous as clouds.
From the time he was held in his mother’s arms until he could be carried about, he was already brilliant and outstanding.

Just as he reached the age for the study of the classics, he achieved a distinguished reputation in the literary garden. Possessing innate wisdom born of celestial endowment, he attained profound understanding from within his own mind, and his scholarly efforts were fully perfected.
He was broad-minded and versatile, excelling among his predecessors; as a gentleman who is not limited to a single function, he was suitable for any role and adaptable to every circumstance.
By keeping his mind empty, he benefited from others' instruction, acting as a mirror that reflects everything without omission—truly receiving all through emptiness.

Because of this vast learning and manifold talents, men of outstanding character yearned for his brilliance and admired him from afar; because his innate wisdom was so clear and penetrating, heroes looked up to him with longing and came to seek refuge in him.
Thus, from the time he reached Bitan until his arrival at Guoqing, his followers were as numerous as clouds. A line from the *Guofeng* (Book of Songs) says: "The daughter of Qi goes to her marriage;

her followers are as numerous as clouds. Bitan was none other than Yi Xing. Guoqing is located on Mount Tiantai. Because he possessed celestial faculties and was profoundly learned, he became the one capable of providing the conditions for questioning the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the Profound Meaning).
△ The second section concerns the circumstances of seeking out [the Dharma] amidst turmoil.

Recently, the island barbarians have raised up difficulties, and the seas and mountains have known no peace. Amidst this abundance of those pursuing the Dharma, some have retreated into mountain retreats;

others say that since their bodies are in peril and the Dharma may perish, it would be better to uphold the Dharma while preserving their lives. Thus, they reluctantly set out on their journey, exposing themselves to the wilds and open fields—this is what they find joy in.
Regarding the Dharma: one should request its increase with joy and compliance.
During the Guangde era of Emperor Daizong, the Tibetan tribes rose in rebellion. Prominent scholars and sages of the Way went into hiding in mountain caves.
Some said to Master Jingxi, "If we remain here, our lives will be in peril and the Dharma will perish; both would be lost. What do you think?"

Fashen attained both [the two goals]. Consequently, he diligently resided among the mountains and wilds; yet those from all quarters who admired his learning also sought his instruction, following him with joy.
Because the world was in turmoil and he could not propagate the teachings widely, those who followed him with joy even engaged in inquiries using bamboo slips.
This is the origin of the practice of "inquiry by slip" (qiānfǎng).
△ Second, the method for composing the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary).

Now, while the Dharma is truly boundless, the physical body is subject to limitations; thus, there has been no leisure to propagate it extensively. However, this sub-commentary provides a reliable basis for inquiry.
By relying on this commentary to provide explanations, one’s thoughts will be set free and one’s efforts redoubled. How magnificent and vast it is!

Jingxi was naturally gifted and possessed vast learning; although the Buddha-dharma he internalized was boundless, his physical body—composed of the five aggregates—could only propagate and expound it by depending on external conditions.
Since the world was in turmoil and people were scattered, the conditions for widespread dissemination were absent;

yet those who delighted in the Dharma and followed him with joy arrived in great numbers, bringing bundles of slips of paper, all seeking to record the profound and hidden points of doubt regarding the *Xuanyi*.
He inquired by means of bamboo slips, and Jingxi, based on the meanings of the questions inscribed upon those slips, provided his explanations.
Since he did not arrange the sequence of the textual arguments in a formal order, his thought was free and unrestrained;

because the meanings of his responses were focused, refined, and precise, his merit was doubled. As Jingxi stated in his own preface: "Following the inquiries of various questioners, [the answers] were recorded beneath the slips."
What has been recorded here does not allow for a leisurely investigation into the development of the textual flow, nor has it yet provided a detailed analysis of the phrasing and punctuation.
This *Zhengxu qian* (Sub-commentary on the Preface) was composed during a time of chaos; immediately following it, he sighed in praise, saying: "How magnificent! How vast!
This *Shiqian* (Commentary on the Sub-commentary) may truly be called one that is perfect in every way and has achieved the great synthesis. There are those who point this out...

To claim that this is a formal eulogy of the *Xuánwén* (Profound Text) is incorrect; it is because the roles of host and guest, as well as the sequence of before and after, are confused and disordered therein.

II. The Circumstances of the Compilation of the *Shìqiǎn* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning). This refers to the passage in the original preface stating: "Returning late to the Vihāra, I have ventured to add superficial embellishments, supplementing them with my own limited views.
Nevertheless, what is recorded here is none other than a recounting of what I have heard, supplemented by my investigations into the sūtras and śāstras; I merely seek to ensure [the transmission]."
"Using concise brevity while being somewhat familiar with the detailed and the abbreviated, I present this to later sages, daring to hope for their emendations and deletions.
This refers to the two [versions]: first, "Transcending the Shore" (Chūō), which requires the cultivation of karmic conditions.

Those who have entered the gate have never encountered the slightest difficulty; those who gaze toward the distant shore feel shame that they themselves cannot reach it. Using this as a lesson, how could the literary expression be discarded?
As for the mechanism of inquiry through divination, there are those who attain realization through its interpretation; since they have never encountered the difficulty of "sticking fast," then this—
It might seem that the *Shiqian* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning) could be dispensed with and need not be included in the compilation;
however, those with the capacity to understand it upon a single hearing are extremely rare. Consequently, there remain many who grieve at their inability to fathom its depths.

Therefore, it is appropriate to preserve this *Shiqian* and compile it as a formal text, so that students may repeatedly unravel and contemplate its contents before they can attain awakening and entry. Thus it is said: "To instruct by means of this text."

It should not be discarded, but rather collected and compiled. "Riding upon" (chéng) means that by relying on a certain person to perform a certain task—just as one relies on hot soup to quench thirst or relies on rice being present to alleviate hunger—the character "chéng" refers to the *Shiqian* (Explanatory Sub-commentary).
It signifies that the text explaining [the meaning] via bamboo slips is present; it should be preserved for the purpose of instruction and edification.
For one who has realized this, [the practice] must not be abandoned. There is an interpretation that takes "zuò" (作) as meaning "cause" (因), but this is incorrect.

Throughout my early years, I remained amidst the secular world; later, I followed the Way. I merely sought to strike at its great principles, yet alone I felt no shame before my own heart.
"Hu" (Ah!)—

It is as clear as the sun and moon. Alas, how can the blindness of men obscure the intent of this preface? The preface concludes.

During the Zhou dynasty, the various feudal states all usurped the title of "King. Therefore, when Confucius composed the *Spring and Autumn Annals*, he referred to the Son of Heaven as the "Heavenly King" (*Tianwang*) to honor him and distinguish him from others.
This is evident in such passages as "The Heavenly King was hunting at Heyang," "The Heavenly King is sagely and enlightened," and "I serve as the Heavenly King," and so forth.
Furthermore, whenever the Son of Heaven traveled on inspection through the four quarters without specific business, upon his arrival—
"Chù" (place) refers to being at the imperial residence; for example, "on such-and-such a day, such-and-such a person went to the imperial residence.
When a state is in turmoil and one flees the chaos, the place one arrives at is called "yuèzài" (being away from); for example, in the *Zuǒzhuan*, "being away in the grass and brush."
During the reign of Emperor Daizong of the Tang dynasty, due to the turmoil caused by the Tibetan incursions, he fled in haste to Xiancheng;
hence the phrase "fleeing afar. As for the year Jiachen of the following year: having fled abroad in the year Gui-mao, this preface was completed in the subsequent year, Jiachen.
